items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1976-02-04
items.q: I knew Louis Armstrong real well... Louis came in, man, and he sat at the table... We all met him and everybody... So I had him, I just picked up the horn and handed him the horn.

ctx.x: I'm Black, and I'm wondering how well you knew Louis Armstrong when he was alive.

I knew Louis Armstrong real well. I got known him from around 19... 20... 27 when I went to Chicago. Lee Collins' band went on an excursion from New Orleans, and Lee and Lurie were buddies from kids. And naturally, Louis, Lee searched Lurie out and went to an excursion which they used to give all during the summer. Illinois Central Railroad, Illinois Railroad would give excursions to Chicago because so many people from New Orleans had relatives in Chicago. And there were always a trainload of people who would go…
First chance I got to see Lurie, but I had...

items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1976-02-04
items.q: Louis stuff was so black out of the Baptist Church and out of the honky tonks... he heard the best he knew... he came out of that which is nitty-gritty black American earth lifestyle.

ctx.x: what was the difference in their style?

Well, there's a big difference. one was lyrical which from, from a classical vein, technically musical because Bix was a, uh, was interested in concert music and Debussy and Ravel and his thing was semi-classical, that In the Mist and a couple of piano pieces he wrote which had a, a great significance of creative inventiveness but based from a European, a classical vein where Louis stuff was so black out of the Baptist Church and out of the honky tonks and, uh, out of, uh, a tradition of New Orleans trumpet…

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Dodds was in Chicago. He was the first one in Chicago to keep the New Orleans tradition other than King Oliver and Louis Armstrong.

ctx.x: The Barbarin family is one of the most popular names in New Orleans music with names like Paul and Louis and Isidore. How is your mother related to them?

That’s her brothers you call. Paul’s a brother. Willie’s a brother. Lucien’s a brother. Paul, Willie, Lucien, and Louis. They all played music, because my whole family . . . We were encouraged to play music, because it added to the poor folk’s moneybag. It added a little money more to the . . . You played as a extra to your regular job, whatever you . . . was your profession or your trade. Mostly your trade. By playing music, you added on weekends or anytime, you added to the moneybags in the family.
So it was an honor to be a musician.

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: And there was Guy Kelly playing identically like Armstrong, and almost looking like Armstrong.

ctx.x: They worked in bands with them.

Yeah, out in Indiana. They joined them bands. There's a picture, you're supposed to see...a painting that's supposed to be Louis Armstrong and Bix Beiderbecke discussing music on a wharf that's by some bales of cotton.
Well, that's what you heard in the evening. Now, other than that, you heard...
